chunks: "Interrupts are great, but they come with limits I'd always keep in mind. First, latency isn't zero and isn't constant.
There's the entry overhead, but the real problem is jitter: if main code disables interrupts for a critical section, or a higher-priority ISR is running, my response waits.
So worst case matters, not average. Second, events can be lost. A peripheral has one pending bit, so if two events occur before I service the first, I only get one interrupt.
And an ISR that's too long causes the next event to be missed. Third, there's overhead.
Every interrupt costs entry and exit, a few hundred nanoseconds, so at hundreds of kilohertz the CPU is swamped. That's when I switch to DMA or timer hardware.
The ISR can run between any two instructions of main code, so shared variables need volatile and atomic access, and bugs are intermittent and hard to reproduce.
Fifth, resources: each ISR uses stack, and nesting multiplies it, and you only have a limited number of priorities and vectors.
Finally, ISRs have restrictions: no blocking, no malloc or printf, and long ISRs hurt everything else. Debugging is also hard because breakpoints change the timing.
The mitigations are short ISRs, deferred processing, careful priorities, DMA for high rates, and hardware paths for hard deadlines."
